2: Because a workload can use its access faster and more widely than any person.
An application permission gives an app everything its scope allows, across the whole tenant.
And a permission like Directory dot ReadWrite dot All, granted to make it work, stays until someone takes it away.
In this module you find those grants and take them away safely.
You sweep every service principal, flag the broad grants without a current exception, and ask the owners.
Two rules hold the whole time.
Nothing is removed until a second person approves the plan's hash.
And the code removes a grant, never an app.
3: Here's what you'll be able to do by the end of this module, which takes about sixty minutes with the lab.

You'll say which service principals go to the Privileged Access plan, and why this chapter doesn't sweep them.

4: Unit 1 is the guide's Step 4, sub-steps four a to four c.
Microsoft Learn's guidance is to prefer delegated access where a user is present, because a delegated grant gives the app only the intersection of the user's rights and the scope.

Learn also says removing a permission from the app registration doesn't revoke an existing grant, and that tokens already issued stay valid for their lifetime.
Microsoft Learn's page on privileged roles calls a service principal with a highly privileged role a control-plane asset.

5: Unit 2 starts with the rule the code holds, which is the program's, so it's design guidance.
Owners review every grant every quarter, and the review closes only when its findings are acted on.
No broad permission stands without a recorded exception, which names a justification, an approver, an approval date and an end date.
Where Microsoft Learn documents a narrower replacement, such as Selected permissions in SharePoint, or role-based access control for applications in Exchange Online, that's the target.
A managed identity's Azure roles belong at the resource, because, as Microsoft Learn's Azure role assignment steps say, a role at a subscription or management group reaches everything under it.
Privileged service principals are handed to the Privileged Access plan.
And the code removes a grant, never the app: one app role assignment through the resource, or one delegated grant narrowed.

7: Two pieces sit between the check and the plan.
Four escalation permissions let an app grant itself more or act as others.

The Microsoft Graph permissions reference cautions that app role assignment read-write and role management read-write can grant authorization, and that application read-write lets an app act as other entities.
And Microsoft Learn's guide to granting permissions says only appropriate users should reach apps granted delegated permission grant read-write.
Any service principal holding one, or holding a directory role, is handed off whole to the Privileged Access plan, with everything it holds listed.
It gets no finding here, so two plans never disagree about it.
It has one row per grant of every service principal that stays here, sent to its owners.
Under the program's design guidance, only decisions dated this quarter count; an earlier answer shows as the last decision, and the row is open again.
The review closes when every row is decided this quarter and nothing approved for removal is still granted.
8: Unit 3 is the plan and the write path.
The plan has one action per broad grant and per decided change, and only two kinds ever write.
Remove app role removes an application permission an owner decided to remove, but only once any named replacement is already granted.
Narrow grant shrinks a delegated grant to a smaller set of scopes, never to nothing.
Everything else is recorded and sends nothing: waiting for a replacement or a decision, kept under an exception, re-scoped by the owner in reviewed infrastructure code, or handed off.
The write path is a separate script.
It runs only the plan whose hash was approved, for this tenant and cloud, no more than seven days old.
It re-reads each target before writing.

And it runs as a person with Privileged Role Administrator, never an unattended app, because, as the Microsoft Graph permissions reference cautions, the write permissions can grant authorization themselves.
The seven-day limit is the program's design guidance.
